analysis.one_liner: Preserves state lawsuits against pesticide makers over labels and packaging.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Agriculture Committee on June 29, 2026, with no committee action since; the 119th Congress is still in session.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal pesticide law so that people can still sue pesticide companies under state law over how their products are labeled or packaged. Federal law currently regulates pesticide labels through the EPA, and the bill adds language making clear that federal rules do not wipe out those state-law injury claims [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to pesticides, including farmworkers, rural residents, and homeowners, who could sue pesticide manufacturers under state law for injuries tied to product labels or packaging. Their lawyers and state courts gain a clearer avenue for these cases.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmworkers, rural residents, and pesticide-exposure victims

how_it_helps.text: Amends Section 24(b) of the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act to state that the federal preemption provision 'shall not be construed to prohibit or otherwise limit a claim related to the labeling or packaging of pesticides or devices under the tort law of any State' [S2].
The bill is titled the 'People Over Poison Act' and its stated purpose is protecting tort claims under state law related to pesticide labeling or packaging [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers, who would face liability in state courts for labeling and packaging claims, and potentially their customers if companies raise prices or change labels to cover legal risk.

drawbacks.text: State-by-state lawsuits over federally approved pesticide labels could create inconsistent liability standards across states, and companies argue they relied on EPA-approved labels in good faith; the practical cost could fall partly on farmers through higher pesticide prices or withdrawn products (general policy mechanism, not sourced).
A single cosponsor and referral only to the Agriculture Committee — the committee with jurisdiction over pesticide law — means the bill has no visible path to a floor vote [S1][S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a legal remedy for people injured by pesticide labels or packaging that federal regulation might otherwise cut off; the cost is greater litigation risk for pesticide makers, some of which could reach farmers as higher prices or fewer product choices. The provision is narrow — it addresses labeling and packaging claims only, not a ban or restriction on any pesticide — but with one cosponsor and no committee action, its practical effect so far is nil.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late June 2026 and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Introduced in the House on June 29, 2026 by Rep. Chellie Pingree, joined by Rep. Thomas Massie [S1][S2].
Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture on the day of introduction; the action history shows no further steps [S4].
The bill has one cosponsor, a Republican, giving it small bipartisan sponsorship [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, pesticide manufacturers, who remain shielded by current federal law from state labeling and packaging suits because the bill has not advanced.

for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 29, 2026 and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — through the present

sides.party_line_note: A Democratic sponsor and a Republican cosponsor introduced it together; no votes have occurred to show a partisan split [S2][S3].

industries.note: The bill strips away the federal preemption that has protected pesticide makers from state tort claims over product labels and packaging, exposing them to jury lawsuits for injuries. Their interest in keeping that shield runs against injured people's interest in having a day in court [S2].
Farmers could face higher prices or fewer products if liability costs rise, but many also live and work where pesticides are applied and could use the same state-law claims when exposed [S2].
They gain a preserved right to sue under state law for injuries tied to pesticide labeling or packaging, the group the bill is written for [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, a late-June introduction in the second session, and a referral to the Agriculture Committee with no follow-up, the likely path is that the bill sits in committee until the Congress ends on January 3, 2027 without a vote.
